senses: It is wiser to be careful now than to take a risk and regret it later.

etymology: An old English proverb; versions such as "better be sure than sorry" go back to the 1800s.

conversation.text: Bring a jacket. It probably won't rain, but better safe than sorry.
I called the bank to confirm the transfer. Better safe than sorry.

core.definition: Take the careful choice, even if it seems unnecessary, because the cost of a mistake would be worse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SORRY most and SAFE a little: better SAFE than SORry. "Than" is reduced to thuhn.

nuance.connotation: Positive and practical; it explains or justifies a small precaution.
nuance.usage_note: Usually said on its own, as a short sentence, right after you mention a precaution: "I backed up my files. Better safe than sorry." It can also follow "It's": "It's better to be safe than sorry." It fits small, everyday precautions best.
word_family: better to be safe than sorry (full form)

distinctions.vs: err on the side of caution
distinctions.note: "Err on the side of caution" describes choosing the careful option and sounds more formal; "better safe than sorry" is the quick spoken reason for it.

distinctions.vs: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure
distinctions.note: Both praise caution, but "an ounce of prevention" is about preventing a bigger problem, often health or maintenance; "better safe than sorry" is about avoiding regret.

collocations: better safe than sorry
it's better to be safe than sorry
just being safe
better safe than sorry, right?

examples.everyday: I put sunscreen on the kids even though it's cloudy. Better safe than sorry.
examples.professional: We added a second reviewer for the payroll changes; better safe than sorry with people's paychecks.
examples.analytical: The precautionary principle in policy is essentially "better safe than sorry": act to prevent serious harm even before the evidence is complete.

nuance.analogy: Like wearing a seatbelt on a short drive: it costs almost nothing, and you'll be glad if something happens.
nuance.etymology: An old English proverb; versions such as "better be sure than sorry" go back to the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying "better sorry than safe"; the safe choice comes first.
Using it for a big, bold decision; it is only for being careful.

senses: When one bad thing happens, other bad things often follow at the same time.
More generally, things tend to happen all at once: several problems, or sometimes several pieces of good news, arrive together.

etymology: From the British proverb "it never rains but it pours" (1700s). The American form became familiar through Morton Salt's slogan of 1914, which advertised that its salt still poured in wet weather.

conversation.text: First the car broke down, then the dishwasher, and now the dog is sick. When it rains, it pours.
No job offers for months, and now I have three in one week. When it rains, it pours!

core.definition: Troubles (or events in general) seem to come all together instead of one at a time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress POURS. "Pours" rhymes with "doors."

nuance.connotation: Rueful and sympathetic; often said with a sigh or a laugh.
nuance.usage_note: Usually a comment on a run of bad luck, said by the person it's happening to or by a sympathetic friend. It is also used humorously for good things arriving at once. Americans may know it from the Morton Salt slogan.
word_family: it never rains but it pours (older, more British form)

distinctions.note: "The last straw" is the final problem that makes you lose patience; "when it rains, it pours" is about many problems arriving close together.
A superstition with a similar idea; "when it rains, it pours" doesn't count the problems.

collocations: when it rains, it pours
well, when it rains, it pours
you know what they say: when it rains, it pours

examples.everyday: The basement flooded the same day I lost my phone. When it rains, it pours.
examples.professional: Two people resigned and our biggest client called with a complaint the same morning; when it rains, it pours.
examples.analytical: The saying "when it rains, it pours" reflects a real pattern: one setback, like a job loss, often causes others, like debt and stress.

nuance.analogy: Like weather: one drop and suddenly you're in a downpour.
nuance.etymology: From the British proverb "it never rains but it pours" (1700s). The American form became familiar through Morton Salt's slogan of 1914, which advertised that its salt still poured in wet weather.
common_mistakes: Saying "when it rains, it rains"; the second verb is "pours."
Using it for a single problem; it is about many things happening at once.

word: the grass is always greener on the other side
phonetic: /ðə ˈɡɹæs ɪz ˌɔlweɪz ˈɡɹinɚ ɑn ðə ˌʌðɚ ˈsaɪd/

senses: People tend to think that other people's situations (jobs, homes, relationships, lives) are better than their own, even when they are not.

etymology: An old proverb with roots in Latin writers; the English wording became popular in the 20th century, helped by a 1920s popular song and a 1960 film titled "The Grass Is Greener."

conversation.text: You think his job is perfect, but he works sixty hours a week. The grass is always greener on the other side.
I wanted to live in the city, and now I miss the quiet. I guess the grass is always greener.

core.definition: What other people have always looks better than what you have, but it often isn't really better.

pronunciation.ipa: /ðə ˈɡɹæs ɪz ˌɔlweɪz ˈɡɹinɚ ɑn ðə ˌʌðɚ ˈsaɪd/
pronunciation.respelling: thuh gras iz awl-wayz gree-ner on thee uh-ther SYDE
pronunciation.tip: The two strongest beats are GRASS and GREENER, then SIDE at the end. People often shorten it to "the grass is always greener."

nuance.connotation: Gently cautionary: it warns against envy and restlessness.
nuance.usage_note: Often shortened to "the grass is always greener." It is used to talk someone out of a change, or to explain disappointment after a change. A common variant is "the grass isn't always greener."
word_family: the grass is always greener (short form)

distinctions.note: "Greener pastures" is a better place or job you move on to, said positively; "the grass is always greener" warns that the better place may be an illusion.
"Keeping up with the Joneses" is competing with neighbors in what you own; "the grass is always greener" is imagining their life is better.

collocations: the grass is always greener on the other side
the grass isn't always greener
grass-is-greener syndrome
classic grass-is-greener thinking

examples.everyday: She left her small town for New York and found out the grass isn't always greener.
examples.professional: Before you take the competing offer, remember the grass is always greener; ask about their hours and turnover.
examples.analytical: Social media can intensify grass-is-greener thinking, because people compare their ordinary days with others' highlights.

nuance.analogy: Like your neighbor's lawn seen from your window: from far away you can't see the weeds.
nuance.etymology: An old proverb with roots in Latin writers; the English wording became popular in the 20th century, helped by a 1920s popular song and a 1960 film titled "The Grass Is Greener."
common_mistakes: Saying "the grass is greener in the other side"; it is "on the other side."
Using it to praise a real improvement; the saying suggests the improvement may be imaginary.

senses: It is very difficult to stop doing something you have done for a long time.

etymology: Recorded in English since the 1700s; "die hard" means to resist dying for a long time.

conversation.text: I'm retired, but I still wake up at 5:30. Old habits die hard.
You still check the fridge every time you walk by? Old habits die hard.

core.definition: Long-standing habits are hard to break, even when you want to change.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HARD most, with a second beat on HABITS. The "h" in "habits" and "hard" is pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to affectionate; often a self-aware, slightly amused comment.
nuance.usage_note: Usually said as a short comment after someone does something out of habit. It is gentle; it explains a habit rather than criticizing it.
word_family: die hard (verb phrase; also die-hard, adjective: a die-hard fan)

distinctions.vs: you can't teach an old dog new tricks
distinctions.note: "You can't teach an old dog new tricks" says older people can't learn new things; "old habits die hard" is about anyone's habits being hard to break.
"Force of habit" explains one action ("I locked it out of force of habit"); "old habits die hard" comments on how lasting habits are.

collocations: old habits die hard
I guess old habits die hard
old habits really do die hard

examples.everyday: Even after moving to Texas, my mom still keeps a snow shovel by the door. Old habits die hard.
examples.professional: The team switched to the new tracking system, but old habits die hard, and some updates still come by email.
examples.analytical: Behavioral research supports the idea that old habits die hard: habits run on automatic cues, so changing them takes repetition, not just willpower.

nuance.analogy: Like a path worn into a lawn: people keep walking on it even after you put in a sidewalk.
nuance.etymology: Recorded in English since the 1700s; "die hard" means to resist dying for a long time.
common_mistakes: Saying "old habits die slowly" or "old habits never die"; the fixed form is "die hard."
Thinking "die hard" means the habit dies easily; it means the opposite.

word: you can't teach an old dog new tricks
phonetic: /ju ˌkænt ˌtitʃ ən ˌoʊld ˌdɔɡ ˌnu ˈtɹɪks/

senses: It is hard or impossible for older or experienced people to learn new skills or change their ways.

etymology: An English proverb recorded since the 1500s, originally in farming books about training dogs.

conversation.text: My grandfather refuses to use a smartphone. You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
I learned to swim at sixty. Who says you can't teach an old dog new tricks?

core.definition: People who have done things one way for a long time find it hard to change or learn something new.

pronunciation.ipa: /ju ˌkænt ˌtitʃ ən ˌoʊld ˌdɔɡ ˌnu ˈtɹɪks/
pronunciation.respelling: yoo kant teech uhn ohld dawg noo TRIKS
pronunciation.tip: Stress TRICKS most, with beats on OLD DOG and NEW. American "can't" is kant, with the vowel of "cat."

nuance.connotation: Mildly teasing; often used jokingly about oneself, or turned around to say it isn't true.
nuance.usage_note: Often used humorously about yourself ("I'm an old dog") or turned around: "Who says you can't teach an old dog new tricks?" Said about another person, especially an older coworker, it can sound dismissive or ageist.
word_family: an old dog (person set in their ways)
teach an old dog new tricks (verb phrase)

distinctions.note: "Old habits die hard" is about breaking habits at any age; "you can't teach an old dog new tricks" is about older people not learning new things.
"Set in one's ways" describes the person directly and plainly: "He's set in his ways."

collocations: you can't teach an old dog new tricks
who says you can't teach an old dog new tricks
an old dog learning new tricks
proof you can teach an old dog new tricks

examples.everyday: My dad finally learned to text with emojis, so you can teach an old dog new tricks.
examples.professional: Don't assume senior staff can't learn the new software; the idea that you can't teach an old dog new tricks is usually wrong.
examples.analytical: Research on adult learning challenges the belief that you can't teach an old dog new tricks; older adults learn well with practice and motivation.

nuance.analogy: Like asking a river to change course: it can happen, but it takes a lot of time and pressure.
nuance.etymology: An English proverb recorded since the 1500s, originally in farming books about training dogs.
common_mistakes: Saying "you can't teach old dogs new tricks" is fine, but "you can't learn an old dog new tricks" is wrong; the verb is "teach."
Using it directly about an older person ("You're an old dog"); it can offend. It is safest about yourself.

word: if it ain't broke, don't fix it
phonetic: /ɪf ɪt ˌeɪnt ˈbɹoʊk ˌdoʊnt ˈfɪks ɪt/

senses: If something is working well, don't change it; changing it could make it worse.

etymology: American; popularized in 1977 by Bert Lance, a U.S. government official, though the idea is older.

conversation.text: Why update the old system? It does the job. If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
Don't add anything to Grandma's chili. If it ain't broke, don't fix it.

core.definition: Leave a working system, method or thing alone instead of changing it just for the sake of change.

pronunciation.ipa: /ɪf ɪt ˌeɪnt ˈbɹoʊk ˌdoʊnt ˈfɪks ɪt/
pronunciation.respelling: if it aynt BROHK dohnt FIKS it
pronunciation.tip: Two stresses: BROKE and FIX. "Ain't" rhymes with "paint." The grammar is deliberately casual; it's part of the saying.

nuance.connotation: Practical and folksy; it can also sound resistant to change.
nuance.usage_note: The nonstandard "ain't broke" is fixed in the saying, and educated speakers use it this way on purpose; "if it isn't broken, don't fix it" sounds stiff. It is common in business and tech talk too. People who want change sometimes answer, "It is broke, though."
word_family: if it isn't broken, don't fix it (standard-grammar variant)

distinctions.note: "Let sleeping dogs lie" means don't stir up an old problem; "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" means don't change something that works.
"Leave well enough alone" is similar but says "good enough" rather than "working well."

collocations: if it ain't broke, don't fix it
the if-it-ain't-broke approach
if it ain't broke, why fix it?

examples.everyday: I've had the same barber for twenty years. If it ain't broke, don't fix it.
examples.professional: The checkout flow converts well, so let's not redesign it this quarter; if it ain't broke, don't fix it.
examples.analytical: An if-it-ain't-broke attitude protects working systems, but it can also hide slow decline until something finally fails.

nuance.analogy: Like a car that starts every morning: you don't take the engine apart just to see if you can make it better.
nuance.etymology: American; popularized in 1977 by Bert Lance, a U.S. government official, though the idea is older.
common_mistakes: "Correcting" it to "if it ain't broken"; the saying uses "broke."
Writing "ain't" in formal writing outside the saying; it is acceptable only inside this fixed phrase.

word: Rome wasn't built in a day

senses: Important things take a long time to achieve, so be patient.

etymology: A medieval proverb, found in French in the 1100s and in English by the 1500s.

conversation.text: You've only played guitar for two weeks. Rome wasn't built in a day.
The garden doesn't look like much yet, but Rome wasn't built in a day.

core.definition: Great or difficult work cannot be finished quickly; it needs time and steady effort.

pronunciation.respelling: ROHM wuz-uhnt bilt in uh DAY
pronunciation.tip: Stress ROME and DAY. "Rome" rhymes with "home"; "wasn't" is WUZ-uhnt.

nuance.connotation: Encouraging; it asks for patience, with oneself or with others.
nuance.usage_note: Used to encourage someone who is frustrated with slow progress, or to defend slow progress: "Give it time. Rome wasn't built in a day." Capitalize "Rome."
word_family: wasn't built in a day (often adapted: my business wasn't built in a day)

distinctions.vs: good things come to those who wait
distinctions.note: "Good things come to those who wait" is about waiting patiently for a reward; "Rome wasn't built in a day" is about patient work.

distinctions.vs: slow and steady wins the race
distinctions.note: "Slow and steady wins the race" says the patient approach beats the fast one; "Rome wasn't built in a day" says big things take time.

collocations: Rome wasn't built in a day
remember, Rome wasn't built in a day
Rome wasn't built in a day, you know

examples.everyday: I'm saving a little each month. Rome wasn't built in a day.
examples.professional: The new sales team won't hit full speed this quarter; Rome wasn't built in a day.
examples.analytical: Lasting institutions, like Rome itself, are built through many small decisions over decades, not by a single plan.

nuance.analogy: Like a brick wall: it goes up one brick at a time, no matter how big the plan is.
nuance.etymology: A medieval proverb, found in French in the 1100s and in English by the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Writing "rome" with a small r; it is the city, so capitalize it.
Saying "Rome wasn't built in one day" is understandable, but the fixed form is "in a day."

word: where there's a will, there's a way
phonetic: /ˌwɛɹ ðɛɹz ə ˈwɪl ðɛɹz ə ˈweɪ/

senses: If someone is determined enough to do something, they will find a way to do it.

etymology: An English proverb recorded since the 1600s in forms like "where the will is ready, the feet are light"; the modern wording dates from the 1800s.

conversation.text: You can finish the degree while working. Where there's a will, there's a way.
He climbed in through the window to get his phone? Well, where there's a will, there's a way.

core.definition: Strong determination finds a solution, even when the obstacles look serious.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌwɛɹ ðɛɹz ə ˈwɪl ðɛɹz ə ˈweɪ/
pronunciation.respelling: wair thairz uh WIL thairz uh WAY
pronunciation.tip: Stress WILL and WAY. "There's" is one syllable: thairz.

nuance.connotation: Positive and motivating; also used wryly about someone's stubborn persistence.
nuance.usage_note: Mostly encouraging. It is also used with a smile about someone who did something odd to get what they wanted. "Will" here means determination, not the future tense or a legal will.

distinctions.note: "Nothing ventured, nothing gained" is about taking a risk; "where there's a will, there's a way" is about determination.
A common way to start the saying and leave it unfinished: "Well, where there's a will..."

collocations: where there's a will, there's a way
where there's a will...
proof that where there's a will, there's a way

examples.everyday: She couldn't afford a car, so she biked ten miles to work. Where there's a will, there's a way.
examples.professional: The budget is tight, but where there's a will, there's a way; let's find savings elsewhere.
examples.analytical: The saying where there's a will, there's a way overstates the case: determination helps, but resources and circumstances also matter.

nuance.analogy: Like water finding a path downhill: if the push is strong enough, it gets around the rocks.
nuance.etymology: An English proverb recorded since the 1600s in forms like "where the will is ready, the feet are light"; the modern wording dates from the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Using "will" to mean a legal document; here it means determination.
Saying "where is a will, is a way"; both halves need "there's."

word: two wrongs don't make a right

senses: Doing something bad to someone because they did something bad to you is not justified.

etymology: An English proverb recorded in the 1700s.

conversation.text: I know he hit you first, but two wrongs don't make a right.
You want to key his car because he dented yours? Two wrongs don't make a right.

core.definition: Answering a wrong with another wrong doesn't fix anything or make it acceptable.

pronunciation.respelling: too RAWNGZ dohnt mayk uh RYTE
pronunciation.tip: Stress WRONGS and RIGHT; the "w" in "wrongs" is silent.

nuance.connotation: Moralizing but gentle; common with children and in arguments.
nuance.usage_note: Said to stop revenge or to answer "But they did it first!" Parents and teachers use it often. It is also used in debates against "whataboutism."

distinctions.note: "An eye for an eye" supports equal punishment; "two wrongs don't make a right" rejects revenge.

distinctions.vs: a taste of one's own medicine
distinctions.note: "A taste of one's own medicine" is getting treated the way you treat others, often enjoyed by others; "two wrongs don't make a right" warns against doing that on purpose.

collocations: two wrongs don't make a right
but two wrongs don't make a right
I know, two wrongs don't make a right

examples.everyday: She lied to me, but two wrongs don't make a right, so I'm not lying back.
examples.professional: Their team broke the agreement, but two wrongs don't make a right; we'll keep our side and raise it formally.
examples.analytical: Pointing to the other side's misconduct does not excuse one's own: two wrongs don't make a right.

nuance.analogy: Like answering a spilled drink by spilling another one: now there are two messes.
nuance.etymology: An English proverb recorded in the 1700s.
common_mistakes: Saying "two wrongs don't make it right"; the fixed form is "make a right."
Spelling "wrongs" without the silent w, or pronouncing the w.

senses: Being too curious, especially about things that are none of your business, can get you into trouble (often a playful way to tell someone to stop asking).

etymology: The older English proverb was "care killed the cat" (care meaning worry), from the 1500s; the "curiosity" form appears in the late 1800s.

conversation.text: "What's in the box?" "Curiosity killed the cat."
Don't open strange email attachments. Curiosity killed the cat.

core.definition: Asking or looking into too much can be dangerous or get you in trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Two stresses: AH in curiOSity and CAT. "Curiosity" has five syllables: kyoor-ee-AH-suh-tee.

nuance.connotation: Usually playful; it can be a gentle brush-off or a real warning.
nuance.usage_note: Very often used to avoid answering a nosy question. A common reply is "...but satisfaction brought it back," which defends curiosity.
word_family: curiosity killed the cat, but satisfaction brought it back (humorous longer form)

distinctions.note: "Mind your own business" is a direct and rude way to say the same thing; "curiosity killed the cat" is softer and playful.
"Let sleeping dogs lie" means don't stir up an old problem; "curiosity killed the cat" warns against snooping.

collocations: curiosity killed the cat
you know what they say about curiosity
but satisfaction brought it back

examples.everyday: He pushed the big red button just to see what it did. Curiosity killed the cat.
examples.professional: I'd avoid digging into the old dispute with that vendor; curiosity killed the cat, and it's settled.
examples.analytical: The proverb curiosity killed the cat reflects an old suspicion of curiosity that modern education largely rejects.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat poking its head into every box and drawer until one day the drawer closes.
nuance.etymology: The older English proverb was "care killed the cat" (care meaning worry), from the 1500s; the "curiosity" form appears in the late 1800s.
common_mistakes: Changing the animal ("curiosity killed the dog"); it is always the cat.
Using it as a serious accusation; it is light and playful.

senses: After failing twice, the third attempt will succeed (said to encourage someone, or after a third try works).

etymology: Origin uncertain; it reflects old beliefs that three is a lucky or magical number. "Charm" here means a magic spell or lucky object.

conversation.text: I failed the driving test twice, but third time's the charm!
"Did the printer work?" "Yes, finally. Third time's the charm."

core.definition: The third try is the lucky one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CHARM. "Third" starts with a soft th (tongue between the teeth).

nuance.connotation: Hopeful and light.
nuance.usage_note: American form. Said before a third try ("Third time's the charm!") or after one works. Sometimes "the third time's the charm." British speakers more often say "third time lucky."

distinctions.note: "Like a charm" means something worked perfectly; "third time's the charm" is about succeeding on the third try.
"If at first you don't succeed, try, try again" encourages trying any number of times; "third time's the charm" points to the third.

collocations: third time's the charm
hopefully third time's the charm
here's hoping third time's the charm
third time was the charm

examples.everyday: The cake fell twice, but third time's the charm; it came out perfect.
examples.professional: We're resubmitting the grant application; third time's the charm.
examples.analytical: "Third time's the charm" reflects a common superstition about the number three found in many cultures.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that finally turns on the third jiggle.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; it reflects old beliefs that three is a lucky or magical number. "Charm" here means a magic spell or lucky object.
common_mistakes: Writing "third times the charm" without the apostrophe; "time's" is short for "time is."
Using it for a first or second try; it refers to the third.

senses: When you are given something for free or have no other options, you should accept what you get without complaining.

etymology: English proverb recorded since the 1500s, as "beggars should be no choosers."

conversation.text: It's a minivan, not a sports car, but beggars can't be choosers. Thanks for the ride!
"The free couch is orange." "Beggars can't be choosers."

core.definition: If you are in need or getting a favor, you can't be picky.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CHOOSERS. "Beggars" is BEG-erz, and "choosers" is CHOO-zerz with a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Wry and self-deprecating when said about yourself; can sound harsh when said to someone in real need.
nuance.usage_note: Most often said about yourself, humorously, when accepting a favor: "Beggars can't be choosers." Said to someone else, it can sound unkind, so use it with friends. It is not about real beggars.

distinctions.vs: don't look a gift horse in the mouth
distinctions.note: "Don't look a gift horse in the mouth" says not to criticize a gift; "beggars can't be choosers" says you can't be picky when you're in need.
"Take it or leave it" is said by the person offering; "beggars can't be choosers" is said by or about the person receiving.

collocations: beggars can't be choosers
well, beggars can't be choosers
hey, beggars can't be choosers

examples.everyday: The only hotel room left had no view, but beggars can't be choosers.
examples.professional: We'd prefer a later time slot for the presentation, but beggars can't be choosers; we'll take the 8 a.m.
examples.analytical: The proverb beggars can't be choosers captures how scarcity removes bargaining power.

nuance.analogy: Like being handed a free umbrella in a storm: you don't complain about the color.
nuance.etymology: English proverb recorded since the 1500s, as "beggars should be no choosers."
common_mistakes: Saying "beggars can't choose"; the fixed form is "can't be choosers."
Using it to describe a homeless person; it is about anyone accepting what they are offered.

senses: Think carefully about the possible results before you do something risky or important.

etymology: An English proverb from the 1300s, popular through Aesop's fable of the fox and the goat in the well.

conversation.text: Moving abroad sounds great, but look before you leap. Visit first.
Before you put your savings into that, look before you leap.

core.definition: Consider the risks and facts before acting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LEAP. "Look" has the short vowel of "book"; "leap" rhymes with "keep."

nuance.connotation: Cautionary and sensible; a bit old-fashioned, like most proverbs.
nuance.usage_note: Used as advice before a big decision. It pairs naturally with "do your homework." "Leap" here is a decision or action, not a real jump.

distinctions.note: "A leap of faith" is acting without proof, often praised; "look before you leap" warns you to check first.
"Better safe than sorry" justifies a precaution; "look before you leap" warns before a decision.

collocations: look before you leap
always look before you leap
a look-before-you-leap approach

examples.everyday: Read the lease carefully before you sign; look before you leap.
examples.professional: Before we commit to the new vendor, let's look before we leap and run a pilot.
examples.analytical: The proverb look before you leap anticipates the formal idea of risk assessment before an irreversible decision.

nuance.analogy: Like checking the depth of the water before you dive.
nuance.etymology: An English proverb from the 1300s, popular through Aesop's fable of the fox and the goat in the well.
common_mistakes: Saying "look before you jump"; the fixed form is "leap."
Changing the pronoun freely is fine: "look before we leap."

word: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure
phonetic: /ən ˈaʊns əv pɹɪˈvɛnʃən ɪz ˌwɝθ ə ˈpaʊnd əv ˈkjʊɹ/

senses: It is easier and cheaper to prevent a problem than to fix it once it happens.

etymology: Popularized by Benjamin Franklin, who wrote it in 1736 about fire safety in Philadelphia.

conversation.text: Get the flu shot. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
Clean the gutters now; an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

core.definition: A small effort to prevent trouble saves a lot of effort, money or pain later.

antonyms: strike while the iron is hot
collocations: that ship has sailed
I think that ship has sailed
that ship sailed a long time ago

examples.everyday: I wanted to be an astronaut, but that ship has sailed.
examples.professional: Changing the launch date now? That ship has sailed; the press release is out.
examples.analytical: Once a market leader is established, competitors often find that the ship has sailed on building a direct rival.

nuance.analogy: Like running to the dock and watching your ship get smaller on the horizon.
nuance.etymology: Late 20th-century American; from the image of arriving at the dock after your ship has left.
common_mistakes: Saying "that ship is sailed"; use "has sailed."
Using it for something still possible; it means the chance is over.

senses: A frustrating situation in which you can't get what you need because of a rule or condition that requires you to already have it.

etymology: From Joseph Heller's 1961 novel "Catch-22," in which a military rule lets pilots avoid combat if they are insane, but asking to avoid combat proves they are sane.

conversation.text: You need experience to get a job, and you need a job to get experience. It's a catch-22.
The bank won't give me a credit card without a credit history. Classic catch-22.

core.definition: A no-win situation created by contradictory rules or conditions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TWO at the end. American "twenty" often sounds like TWEN-ee in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Frustrated; it criticizes illogical systems.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "a catch-22" or "a catch-22 situation." It is a precise term: the two conditions depend on each other. Capitalized as "Catch-22" when referring to the novel.

distinctions.vs: between a rock and a hard place
distinctions.note: "Between a rock and a hard place" is choosing between two bad options; "a catch-22" is when rules make the goal impossible.
"A vicious circle" is a cycle where problems make each other worse; "a catch-22" is a trap made by rules.

collocations: a catch-22
a catch-22 situation
classic catch-22
it's a real catch-22

examples.everyday: I can't rent an apartment without a local address, and I can't get a local address without an apartment: catch-22.
examples.professional: New vendors can't bid without a past contract with us, which is a catch-22 we should fix.
examples.analytical: Economists describe the poverty trap as a catch-22: people need savings to invest in education, and education to earn savings.

nuance.analogy: Like a door that only opens if you're already inside.
nuance.etymology: From Joseph Heller's 1961 novel "Catch-22," in which a military rule lets pilots avoid combat if they are insane, but asking to avoid combat proves they are sane.
common_mistakes: Using it for any difficult situation; it is specifically a situation where the conditions contradict each other.
Writing "catch 22" without a hyphen; the standard form is "catch-22."

senses: Something unpleasant, such as a disappointment or hard truth, that you have to accept.

etymology: From the old practice of coating bitter medicines with sugar; "bitter pill" as a figure of speech dates back to the 1500s.

conversation.text: Not getting into my first-choice school was a bitter pill to swallow.
Losing in the last second was a bitter pill to swallow.

core.definition: A painful fact or outcome that is hard to accept.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BITTER and SWALLOW. American "bitter" has a flap: BID-er.

nuance.connotation: Sad and serious.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "a bitter pill to swallow" or "a hard pill to swallow." It is used about defeats, rejections, criticism and bad news.

distinctions.note: "Bite the bullet" is forcing yourself to do something unpleasant; "a bitter pill to swallow" is something unpleasant to accept.
"The last straw" is a final problem that makes you lose patience; "a bitter pill to swallow" is a painful thing to accept.

collocations: a bitter pill to swallow
a hard pill to swallow
a tough pill to swallow

examples.everyday: Admitting I was wrong in front of everyone was a bitter pill to swallow.
examples.professional: The layoffs were a bitter pill to swallow for a company that had never cut jobs before.
examples.analytical: Austerity measures are often a bitter pill to swallow politically, even when economists agree they are needed.

nuance.analogy: Like medicine that tastes awful but has to go down anyway.
nuance.etymology: From the old practice of coating bitter medicines with sugar; "bitter pill" as a figure of speech dates back to the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying "a bitter pill to eat"; the verb is "swallow."
Using it for something physical; it is about accepting bad news.

word: have one's cake and eat it too
phonetic: /ˌhæv wʌnz ˈkeɪk ən ˈit ɪt ˌtu/

senses: To want or try to get two good things that cannot both be had, because getting one means losing the other.

etymology: An English proverb since the 1500s, originally "wolde you bothe eate your cake, and have your cake?"; the American form often ends with "too."

conversation.text: You want to save money and buy a new car? You can't have your cake and eat it too.
He wants a raise but less responsibility. He wants to have his cake and eat it too.

core.definition: To enjoy two benefits that are not compatible.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌhæv wʌnz ˈkeɪk ən ˈit ɪt ˌtu/
pronunciation.respelling: hav wunz KAYK uhn EET it too
pronunciation.tip: Stress CAKE and EAT. In use, "one's" becomes your, his, her.

nuance.connotation: Critical, often of someone who wants everything without sacrifice.
nuance.usage_note: Usually negative: "You can't have your cake and eat it too," or "She wants to have her cake and eat it too." The logic: once you eat the cake, you no longer have it.

distinctions.note: "Have it both ways" means the same and is a bit plainer.
"The best of both worlds" is positive: really getting two benefits; "have one's cake and eat it too" says you can't.

collocations: you can't have your cake and eat it too
wants to have his cake and eat it too
have their cake and eat it

examples.everyday: You can't stay up all night and feel rested in the morning. You can't have your cake and eat it too.
examples.professional: Leadership wants faster releases with no extra QA staff; they want to have their cake and eat it too.
examples.analytical: Trade-off analysis is the formal version of "you can't have your cake and eat it too": every choice has a cost.

nuance.analogy: Like wanting to keep your money and spend it at the same time.
nuance.etymology: An English proverb since the 1500s, originally "wolde you bothe eate your cake, and have your cake?"; the American form often ends with "too."
common_mistakes: Thinking it is about eating dessert; it is about incompatible choices.
Saying "eat your cake and have it" is the older order; Americans normally say "have your cake and eat it too."

word: the proof is in the pudding

senses: The real value or quality of something can only be judged by trying or using it, not by what people say about it.

etymology: From "the proof of the pudding is in the eating," recorded in the 1600s; "proof" here means test.

conversation.text: The ads say it cleans everything. Well, the proof is in the pudding.
Your diet plan sounds great, but the proof is in the pudding. Let's see in a month.

core.definition: Judge something by its results.

pronunciation.respelling: thuh PROOF iz in thuh PUD-ing
pronunciation.tip: Stress PROOF and PUDDING. "Pudding" has the vowel of "put": PUD-ing.

nuance.connotation: Skeptical but fair.
nuance.usage_note: The original and fuller form is "the proof of the pudding is in the eating." In American English the short "the proof is in the pudding" is the usual form, even though it makes less literal sense.
word_family: the proof of the pudding is in the eating (original form)

distinctions.note: "Actions speak louder than words" is about judging people by what they do; "the proof is in the pudding" is about judging anything by results.
"Seeing is believing" means you will believe it when you see it; "the proof is in the pudding" means results will show the truth.

collocations: the proof is in the pudding
the proof of the pudding is in the eating
as they say, the proof is in the pudding

examples.everyday: The new coach talks a big game, but the proof is in the pudding: let's see how the team plays.
examples.professional: The software looks good in the demo, but the proof is in the pudding; let's run a pilot.
examples.analytical: The proof is in the pudding: an educational program should be judged by student outcomes, not by its design.

nuance.analogy: Like judging a recipe by tasting the dish, not by reading the cookbook.
nuance.etymology: From "the proof of the pudding is in the eating," recorded in the 1600s; "proof" here means test.
common_mistakes: Thinking "proof" means evidence that pudding exists; it means "test," as in "proving" something works.
Using it for a situation where results are already known; it suggests waiting for results.

senses: If the worst possible situation happens (used to describe a backup plan).

etymology: Recorded since the 1500s as "if the worst come to the worst"; the "worse" form is an American variant from the 1700s.

conversation.text: If worst comes to worst, we can sleep in the car.
If worse comes to worst and we miss the flight, there's another at six.

core.definition: In the worst case; if everything goes wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress both WORST. Many Americans say "if worse comes to worst," which sounds almost the same.

nuance.connotation: Reassuring; it introduces a fallback plan.
nuance.usage_note: Usually followed by a backup plan: "If worst comes to worst, I'll call my parents." Both "if worst comes to worst" and "if worse comes to worst" are common in American English. "Worst-case scenario" is a close noun phrase.
word_family: if worse comes to worst (common variant)

distinctions.note: "When push comes to shove" means when a situation becomes urgent and action is needed; "if worst comes to worst" introduces a backup plan.
"At worst" states the worst outcome briefly ("At worst, we lose a day"); "if worst comes to worst" introduces what you would do.

collocations: if worst comes to worst
if worse comes to worst
worst comes to worst, we'll...

examples.everyday: If worst comes to worst, I'll order pizza.
examples.professional: If worst comes to worst and the vendor is late, we'll ship the older version.
examples.analytical: Contingency planning asks what to do if worst comes to worst, so teams can act quickly instead of improvising.

nuance.analogy: Like packing an umbrella just in case: if it pours, you're ready.
nuance.etymology: Recorded since the 1500s as "if the worst come to the worst"; the "worse" form is an American variant from the 1700s.
common_mistakes: Saying "if the worse comes to the worst" in American English; Americans drop "the."
Using it for a good outcome; it is only for a bad one.
